rows.question: What did he work on at Sansar?
rows.answer: At Sansar (Linden Lab), Washington worked as a Game Developer on a contract through BairesDev, remotely, in 2022 [1][4]. He built avatar interaction mechanics and a dynamic animation system for the social VR platform [2], and he optimized shaders and materials, reducing memory usage by about 40% [1][4]. His LinkedIn profile also lists testing new spatial audio features during this contract, which ran from July to November 2022 [4].

rows.question: What is SkyNest?
rows.answer:
SkyNest is a multiplayer VR combat sandbox that Washington is developing; it is still in development [1]. Its features include physics-based hands, melee and ranged weapons, armor with durability, and grenades, plus PvP duels on a self-hosted game server [1]. It is built with Unity 6, Meta Quest, Netcode for GameObjects, and Laravel + React [1]. Washington also made a passwordless account flow that works entirely inside VR, an admin panel, and a backend deployed to a VPS with GitHub Actions [1].

For more details, see his LinkedIn profile: https://www.linkedin.com/in/wxquevedo

- **AR Research Engineer (2020):** He led the migration research from Vuforia to Unity AR Foundation, unifying ARKit/ARCore object recognition and validating cross-platform 3D detection [2][3].

rows.question: Has he published research on VR rehabilitation using haptic devices?
rows.answer:
Yes. Washington has published several papers on VR rehabilitation involving haptic devices:

- **2018 (AVR, Springer LNCS):** A haptic stimulation glove for fine motor rehabilitation in virtual reality, using flexibility sensors and vibratory actuators for feedback, integrated with Unity 3D, Oculus Rift and Leap Motion [1]. This paper has 28 Google Scholar citations as of October 2026 [1].
- **2016 (ISVC):** Upper limb rehabilitation with force feedback, using the Novint Falcon haptic device within a Unity3D virtual reality system [2]. It has 29 citations as of October 2026 [2].

He also worked on a related 2018 paper on a virtual rehabilitation system using a functional hand orthosis, though that one uses a Myo armband rather than a haptic device [5].

rows.question: Which of his papers compared WebGL and WebVR performance?
rows.answer:
Washington has two papers that compare WebGL-related performance:

- "Performance evaluation of WebGL and WebVR apps in VR environments," published at the International Symposium on Visual Computing (ISVC) in 2019. It evaluates devices and browsers running WebGL and WebVR applications, finding similar performance on PCs and a notable advantage for WebVR on mobile devices [1].
- "Performance of WebGL standard for displaying 3D applications on mobile devices," published at the IEEE CISTI conference in 2021. It analyzes how compression formats, connection speeds and browsers affect loading times, performance and build size on mobile devices [2].

Only the first paper directly compares WebGL and WebVR; the second focuses on WebGL alone [1][2].

rows.question: What is My Style AR?
rows.answer: My Style AR is an augmented reality application proposed in a 2018 paper titled "Augmented reality as a new marketing strategy," presented at the International Conference on Augmented Reality, Virtual Reality and Computer Graphics [2]. It lets users preview furniture in real time, such as living room, dining room, and bedroom pieces, and modify size, color, and texture before buying [2]. It also displays relevant product information as items are viewed and changed, aiming to reduce user uncertainty [2]. The app is designed for handheld devices that support augmented reality level 2.0 [2].

rows.question: Has he done any work on eye tracking or gaze estimation?
rows.answer:
Yes. Washington has worked on eye tracking and gaze estimation in at least two ways:

- **Research:** He co-authored "System of evaluation for reading based on eye tracking," a 2017 paper presented at the Emerging Technologies for Education symposium (Springer LNCS). It describes a non-invasive system using a Tobii Eye Tracking sensor to evaluate students during reading or visual appreciation, with results shown as gaze trajectories and statistical weighting [1].

- **Open-source project:** He built Gazetrack, a webcam-based gaze tracker. It uses MediaPipe Face Mesh for head pose, an ETH-XGaze ResNet-18 model on CUDA to estimate gaze direction, and a regularized polynomial regression to map gaze to screen coordinates, with a One-Euro filter for smoothing [2][3][4].

For more of his background, see his LinkedIn profile: https://www.linkedin.com/in/wxquevedo

rows.question: What is Plan Vivo?
rows.answer:
Plan Vivo is a project plan kept in one JSON file (`plan.json`) that AI coding agents keep up to date, paired with a local live viewer that shows phases, real time spent per actor, and a calibrated projection of when the work will finish [2]. It is built to answer questions such as what is done, what is waiting on a human, and how long steps really took compared to estimates [1].

Key features include:

- A single plan format split into phases, with items of type `prompt`, `gate` and `unplanned` [1].
- A React viewer that reloads automatically when `plan.json` is saved [1].
- A `tiempos` command that rebuilds time per actor from Claude Code session logs and `git log` [1].
- Projection of remaining work using a calibration factor based on finished items [1].
- One install per machine that can serve several projects [1].

Washington's repository is available on GitHub at plan-vivo-kit [4]. For more about Washington's work, see his LinkedIn profile: https://www.linkedin.com/in/wxquevedo

rows.question: How does the Localia platform make sure GPU worker results are not lost?
rows.answer: The sources say Localia guarantees result delivery by using Redis `BLMOVE` instead of `BLPOP`. The listener moves each message into a processing list and removes it only after it has been handled, so a dropped connection right after the pop does not lose it [3][5]. Leftover messages are recovered on restart, and TCP keepalive is enabled to detect dead connections behind NAT [3]. The worker pushes results to `localia:results`, which the `worker:listen-results` Artisan command consumes [2][4]. The design came from an earlier issue where a message was lost after a listener dropped the connection following a pop [3].

rows.question: Tell me about his forex trading system project.
rows.answer:
Washington built a personal research project called the Forex Trading System, a platform for designing, backtesting, validating and running algorithmic forex strategies on MetaTrader 5 [1]. It combines a Laravel and React web app with a Python FastAPI bridge to the MT5 terminal [1][3].

Key components include:

- **Strategy engine:** 15 parameterised strategy types, versioned in the database [2].
- **Event-driven backtester:** written in pandas, modelling costs, stop-losses and risk-percent sizing [2].
- **Strategy Explorer and Optimizer:** grid searches ranked on out-of-sample results, with walk-forward validation [2][5].
- **Live bot (demo):** runs strategies through MT5 with daily loss limits, circuit breakers and a news filter [4].
- **Operations tooling:** Telegram alerts, a Windows watchdog and a desktop control panel [3][4].

The project states it is not financial advice and does not claim any strategy is profitable [1].

For more on his work, see https://www.linkedin.com/in/wxquevedo

rows.answer: The Agent Office Visualizer's state engine tracks a catalog of 21 states [2]. The project is an extension of claude-office by Paul Robello and contributors (MIT), and the first 232 commits of its repository are that upstream history [1].

rows.question: ¿Qué tecnologías usa su aplicación sobre la hipótesis de Riemann?
rows.answer:
La aplicación sobre la hipótesis de Riemann es una app web estática construida con React y TypeScript, y los gráficos interactivos se calculan en vivo en el navegador; los ceros de la función zeta se precalculan offline en Python [1]. Está organizada con Vite y React Router (con enrutado por hash), y usa Plotly para los gráficos de líneas, KaTeX para las fórmulas, un shader GLSL en WebGL para la coloración de dominio, y Canvas2D para la animación de la fórmula explícita [3].

Para el cálculo offline, se usa mpmath con 30 cifras decimales, y las pruebas de la parte de Python se hacen con un script de validación [2][5]. Las pruebas unitarias del lado TypeScript se ejecutan con Vitest, y el linter es oxlint [2]. El estado de progreso y el tema claro/oscuro se guardan en el navegador mediante `localStorage` [3].

Si necesitas más detalles sobre su experiencia profesional, puedes consultar su perfil de LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/wxquevedo
